q: A 2-year-old has fever of 39.4 °C, refuses to stand and holds the right hip flexed and externally rotated. WBC is 18 000/mm³ and ESR 65 mm/h. The most appropriate next step is:
o: Oral ibuprofen and review in 48 hours
Ultrasound-guided hip aspiration and surgical drainage with IV antibiotics
X-ray of the pelvis and discharge
MRI of the hip next week
e: All four Kocher criteria are present: septic arthritis is very likely; the hip is aspirated and washed out, and IV antibiotics are started.

q: The commonest organism causing septic arthritis in children of all ages is:
e: Staph aureus is commonest at all ages; Kingella in under-4s; Salmonella in sickle cell disease.

q: A 6-year-old boy has limped for 2 days, one week after a cold. He is afebrile, playful and bears weight. Hip rotation is mildly painful; WBC and ESR are normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
e: A well child after a viral illness, bearing weight, with normal markers: transient synovitis.

q: A 13-year-old obese boy has had knee pain and a limp for 3 weeks. When the hip is flexed, the leg rolls into external rotation. The best investigation is:
o: X-ray of both hips including frog-leg lateral views
e: Classic SCFE: hip pain referred to the knee; frog-leg lateral views show the slip.

q: In Perthes disease, which hip movements are limited first?
e: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head limits abduction and internal rotation.

q: Acute osteomyelitis in a child with sickle cell disease is characteristically caused by:
e: Salmonella is the classic organism in sickle cell disease; ceftriaxone covers it.

q: In acute osteomyelitis, the plain X-ray usually becomes abnormal after:
e: Periosteal reaction appears after 10–14 days; MRI is the best early test.

q: All of the following are features of growing pains EXCEPT:
o: Pain in the evening or at night
e: A limp, morning pain or one-sided pain are red flags that exclude growing pains.

q: A 9-year-old has a painful swollen knee 2 weeks after bloody diarrhoea. Joint fluid is sterile. The diagnosis is:
e: Sterile arthritis 1–4 weeks after a gut infection is reactive arthritis.

q: A child treated for septic arthritis still has fever and a rising CRP after 72 hours of IV antibiotics. The next step is:
o: Repeat imaging and re-drain the joint, review the culture
e: Persistent fever means undrained pus, adjacent osteomyelitis or a resistant organism.
